comment_text.value:
Sorry, but I have been Roman Catholic for 54 years. I've deeply studied the liturgy, architecture, iconography and sacred art. I can assure you that I know "the concept of symbolism" pretty damn well by now.

My mom has a little American flag pin, and she's taken to wearing it inverted on purpose. At least one friend has tried to rotate it right-side up for her, and she had to explain what she's doing with it. I respectfully disagree. My father faithfully flew our flag on every prescribed day, very respectfully, and Dad, (unlike Mom) taught me a lot of respect for authority that was wasted on me in youth, but is beginning to make sense as I age and accumulate more wisdom.

So no, it's not "patriotic" to fly an inverted American flag. It's arrogant. It takes the idea that "our nation is in distress" and leaves it to the judgement of the individual who hoists the flag, rather than our leadership or someone in authority. That's not for us to judge. That's the arrogance.

It's foolish to abuse our national symbol like that. It's disrespectful. It's like calling 9-1-1 to order a pizza. It's not something that patriots do. Patriots fly the flag with respect, and according to the regulations. There are regulations for flying and displaying the American flag.

I've seen a guy at church with a big American flag shirt. It's got eagles and woo woo on it but it's substantially an image of a big American flag, but on his shirt. That's disrespectful. I am sure that he considers himself a patriot, and a conservative, but that is not how Americans should be displaying the flag, as a garment, as wrapping ourselves in something, and certainly not inverting it.

Now if the American flag is flown, inverted, outside an official's residence, such as one of the Supreme Court Justices, perhaps that should be taken with some gravitas. Unfortunately, that very Justice denied that he authorized that display, and apparently his wife did it without his input. So we are kinda back at the arrogance and judgementalism that individual citizens believe our nation is in distress, and therefore, they stretch symbolism to its breaking-point, in order to make a public statement. It's wrong.

I encourage you to try and dial 9-1-1 to order your next pizza, and see how the dispatcher treats you. And now imagine that some veteran comes home from deployment and sees your asinine "symbolism" in your front yard. Perhaps you might care to spit in her face, or give her a slap while you're at it?

comment_text.value:
The Eugene CAHOOTS team has existed since 1989 until it was shut down recently. Dispatchers make the call as to whether or not to send police officers along with CAHOOTS responders on a per call basis.

Quoting vera.org: “ Of the estimated 24,000 calls CAHOOTS responded to in 2019, only 311 required police backup, and in Eugene, CAHOOTS teams resolved almost 20 percent of all calls coming through the city’s public safety communications center.”

To the best of my knowledge, no CAHOOTS staff have died or been seriously injured on the job. I’m not sure the evidence shows that finding the right balance is dangerous. Hard for sure, CAHOOTS put a lot of effort into building the right relationship with the police, but the risk to responders is overstated.

comment_text.value:
The OS overrides location service settings during emergency calls

> When using Emergency SOS to call emergency services, the call may include your location, regardless of whether you enable Location Services, to allow the dispatcher to assist you.

https://www.apple.com/legal/privacy/data/en/emergency-sos/

Android has a similar feature.

There is no legislation requiring this of device (or OS) vendors, but carriers are legally required to make location information available to emergency services, and I think are even prohibited from connecting phones that don’t make this possible. So market forces effectively ensure that all phones do this.

The exception is when the call is too short to get a lock for GPS and location can’t be determined. The phone will still transmit what it can (say, WiFi proximity derived location). Worse case is fall through to carrier triangulation.

More accurately, 112 is the EU emergency number (and the GSM standard) but actual organization of emergency services is entirely national so who deals with your call and how will be local. The article also points out that handling of 911 is local in the US, even if apparently most 911 dispatchers are somehow subordinate to the police.

Also, like 112 forwards to 911 in the US, most cell networks in the EU will forward 911 to 112. American cultural dominance has made it so everyone knows 911 and even Europeans apparently end up dialing it.

comment_text.value:
Basically, 9-1-1 Dispatch relies on the fact that it's a grievous crime and very unglamorous to make a fake report or troll the operator. 9-1-1 needs to remain as credulous as possible, and err on the side of false positives, lest they gain a negative public image.

At the same time, it costs nothing to pick up the phone and prank them. Any actor from anywhere could do it, and outside their jurisdiction, what can they do? The dispatcher is not empowered or equipped to discern truth from lies over a mere voice line from a stranger. The dispatcher can't even run a CAPTCHA to trap AIs. The public absolutely relies on being believed when they sincerely call that same voice line.

I do, perversely, see the merit in repeated response that simply turns out to be a drill. The merit is both training and public image, if the militarized police want to instill fear and shock and awe in that neighborhood, or on the evening news, then they get it by responding, not by dismissing obvious fakes. How often do you get to test your flash-bang rifle, fire up your bomb-siege-robots, and put a few miles on your urban tanks? It's like a parade on your wedding day, but you've already paid.

Only thing is, there seems to be no financial incentive or reward for the SWATter. Unless SWATting could be used to tie up and distract law enforcement resources as part of a bigger conspiracy, the only endgame of SWATting seems to be a drain on resources.

comment_text.value:
> The fire department put together a reunion with the dispatcher, me, my gf, the firefighters that arrived first and did the whole thing, and the EMT team, because they say it’s not often someone survives full cardiac arrest outside a hospital.

Witnessed and early compressions saved her life.

Depending on where you are in the country, even then, your chances of survival vary greatly based on where you are. NY? 11%. Detroit? 7%.

Want to survive? Have your out of hospital arrest witnessed, early compressions and defib, and have it happen in Rochester County MN, King County WA, Pierce County WA or Thurston County WA, where the numbers are in the 40s generally, and those four counties typically are the top 4, though in varying order year to year.

In many cases, what happens is that your normal sinus rhythm degenerates into a shockable rhythm (VF/VT, with an AED, paramedics may manually shock other rhythms), and then, from there, into other worse rhythms (PEA - pulseless electrical activity, asystole) which are generally much harder to come back from. Even with multiple shocks, or ROSC (return of spontaneous circulation), re-arrest is very common, because we've only really "rebooted" the heart, not solved the underlying problem, which is why the other factor in cardiac arrest survival of those origins is "door to balloon time" (i.e. from arrival in the ED to a stent being placed in the cath lab).

Stented within an hour is excellent - the current "gold standard" is still <90m, though most leading hospitals are (and should, it's already more the case in Europe) pushing for D2B of <60m.

story_title.value: How to save a life without knowing CPR

comment_text.value:
My 45 year old gf went from saying she wants to skip work and go to the doctor, to passing out into a wall within 10 minutes. She went into full cardiac arrest and went into the wall so hard she broke the drywall with her head.

I called 911, ran outside to get the address while it rang, and after 30+ seconds answer I g questions and answering questions (which felt like 2+ minutes at the time), they had me start CPR. Never taken a class before.

Paramedics arrived 7 minutes later.

They used an automated chest compression machine, shocked her many times, and got some kind of signal.

Arrived to the ER still in code blue.

Turns out it was a SCAD event. 90% of women that have one die even if they get cpr.

Somehow my gf made it, and was released to home 3 days later after 2 days in the ICU. She had a stent installed within an hour of getting to the ER.

The fire department put together a reunion with the dispatcher, me, my gf, the firefighters that arrived first and did the whole thing, and the EMT team, because they say it’s not often someone survives full cardiac arrest outside a hospital.

story_title.value: How to save a life without knowing CPR

comment_text.value:
> Uber is another key villain in Gouged. Per Owens, Uber’s “greatest innovation wasn’t ‘disrupting’ the taxi industry—it was socializing and normalizing the very idea of dynamic pricing. They made us comfortable with the notion that prices could change at any moment.”

In my opinion, Uber has several key innovations over traditional taxi services:

* An accurate machine-provided fare quote that you can review at your leisure before agreeing to take a trip. (Instead of, like, calling a human dispatcher to ask for a quote.)

* The fact that the passenger can't screw over the driver by making fake requests and not showing up, or running off at the end of a trip - because the online platform is in charge of the payment collection.

* The fact that the driver can't screw the passenger over by driving extra distance, because the price is set ahead of time.

> roughly 75 percent of the items in identical Instacart baskets purchased at the same time varied in price from one shopper to the next

If the price differential is large enough, it sets up an opportunity for arbitrage. Maybe if 10 people cooperate and compare notes on each of their Instacart account's product prices, and then make group purchases using the account with the lowest prices...

In general, it's harder (though not impossible) to price-discriminate on goods rather than services. If seniors get a grocery discount for example, then it might be worthwhile to hire a senior to purchase things on your behalf.

story_title.value: The End of a Fair Price: Dynamic Pricing and the Normalization of Gouging

comment_text.value:
Sorry, but this is incorrect (Restate founder here)

(1) You can model the equivalent of local activities and activities that run on other workers in Restate.

A local activity is a step in the workflow function. An activity supposed to run on a different worker is a function called by the workflow function. Since these calls are just Restate events, exactly-one, suspendable, this gives you a full-fledged workflow/remote-activity pattern. Including concurrency, separate retry policies, etc.

(2) Restate steps commit individually, unlike local activities.

Imagine a two-step workflow, where you want one step durable before starting the second. Account withdrawal before deposit. Restate steps allow you to do that, each step is durable committed before the next step runs.

Per Temporal's own docs, Temporal Local Activity results become durable only when the enclosing Workflow Task completes. That's different than Restate, which can durably commit every individual ctx.run before proceeding to the next step.

Making actual durable commits fast, so you can have sequences of fast durable steps building on each other is super valuable. If an agent can commit the guardrail evaluation in low milliseconds before it starts the tool call, that's great, do it. If committing this involves dispatching another workflow or activity task, the consideration is harder.

When we see someone migrate a Temporal workflow, they often end up using many more durable steps in Restate than they used activities before.

(3) Why do we consider it flexible?

(a) Virtual Objects: Keep state around across the workflow, without doing tricks like "keep the workflow running, signal only, continue_as_new" after a while. Virtual Objects are a natural way to model concurrent stateful entities.

(b) non-workflow communication patterns: We have seen users build lot's of different patterns. It can get as crazy as graphs of functions/objects sending each other durable messages. All end-to-end idempotent (or exactly once, for Virtual Object state). That is outside the hierarchical workflow/subworkflow/activity abstraction.

(4) availability and stability

I don't know where the perception with stability comes from, Restate pushes some pretty high volumes for customers, like 100k+ actions/sec.

The push model in Restate is internally dispatched through queues as well. The application just don't see it as task queues. Limits are implemented through virtual-queues in Restate 1.7.

-----

Of course the systems make different trade-offs. The Restate design (vqueues, push model) is took us longer to build than a task queue model would have, because it puts more work onto the dispatcher that is otherwise handled just implicitly by the worker pools.

But once it is there, it is sooo nice, in how easy it integrates into infra, and how it can handle flow-control with high hierarchical limits in ways I genuinely haven't seen in any other system achieve (see https://restate.dev/blog/announcing-restate-1-7 )

story_title.value: Temporal raises $550M at a $12.55B valuation

comment_text.value: I’m very close with several current police dispatchers, and even have an expired state telecommunicator certification. Calling 911 can absolutely be a coercive force, and people use 911 to harass people all the time because in many instances the dispatcher has no choice but to send uniformed people over there to investigate. Police are equipped and trained to deal with certain kinds of problems, and they’re constantly looking for evidence to support a criminal charge. It’s their job. All they know walking into that situation— as human beings that aren’t immune to the power of suggestion— is that the caller, who is the complainant, says that the other person is doing something wrong. That is not a neutral action. If it was, many departments wouldn’t be adopting non-uniformed, unarmed social worker responses to non-violent situations.

story_title.value: Flock worker calls police on reporter filming public camera installation

comment_text.value:
Specialty sources, the ones people in the affected industry read, tend to be reasonably accurate, because their readership knows the subject and will notice errors. If you want to know which data centers in Dubai were hit by Iranian attacks, the mainstream press and Dubai influencers are useless, but there are data center status sites that have solid info. If you want to know what's getting through the Strait of Hormuz, the info from politicians is useless, but there are shipping sites that name ships and keep stats. If you want to know where GPS is being jammed, there's a tracker site run for aircraft dispatchers. If you want to know what's going on with "return to office", there are commercial real estate sites that have a good idea, including one that gets data from office building entry systems.

Hence looking at Beef Magazine for info about beef.

No, I'm not going to post links. Do your own work. Or get an LLM to do it for you.

comment_text.value:
To be clear the happy path for taxis for me was fine. When things worked things were quite smooth. But this thread is primarily about when things went off the happy path. If a taxi didn't show up, I'd usually have a disinterested dispatcher to talk with who might be able to send another in a half hour. If a taxi intentionally went the long way around to charge more, I'd have to have an argument with the cabbie about this and maybe things would go well maybe they wouldn't. While I didn't personally experience harassment from cabbies I definitely know people who have. So on and so forth. In all of these cases off the happy path the usual recourse back then was worse than the recourse today with e.g. Uber.

Again the overwhelming majority of my taxi rides were fine. The overwhelming majority of my Uber rides are also fine. But when things go wrong they definitely went wrong worse with taxis than Uber rides for me.
